messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventy‑seven years after a deployment in the Gulf, retired Army medic Daniel—whose life had been organized around routine and precision—was in a city hospital when a truck, drunk and out of control, smashed into the ambulance bay, igniting a spray of black‑burnt gasoline that still stains the walls of the waiting room. He remembers the impact as a jagged flash of white light, the hiss of twisted metal, and the sudden, overpowering smell of alcohol that lingers in the air of the bay, a scent that later becomes a trigger whenever he hears the clink of a beer bottle. The vivid crash imagery, the burnt odor, and the echo of an alarm all swirl in his mind, but he finds himself unable to describe the exact sequence of events, the thread of his thoughts dissolving as soon as he tries to speak. He feels the memory as if it belongs to someone else, and occasionally the words “engine cranked” and “sirens blared” surface in his head like a foreign soundtrack. These memories provoke a surge of physical reactivity—heart racing, muscles tensing—making him jump at ordinary sounds, even the murmur of a receptionist’s voice. Because he blames himself for the crash, believing the only way it happened was due to something he did wrong, he develops a harsh inner voice that convinces him he is weak and incapable. The self‑doubt that follows keeps him from trusting his own judgment, and the belief in his own weakness reinforces the belief that he is always in danger. The negative appraisal that the event was his fault keeps him on high alert for any potential trigger. Soon after the accident, the smell of alcohol in any context—a bartender offering a drink, a kitchen smelling of beer—sets off the same physical reactivity he felt on that fateful night, as if the body was recalling the crash. The flash of the wreck, the burnt odor, and the taste of spilled beer together bring the memory rushing back with alien clarity, and the sudden startle response feels automatic. He learns that whenever a trigger appears, his threat response spikes, and he can no longer control the intensity of his thoughts; he starts monitoring them compulsively, checking every sentence for signs of “going crazy.” The very act of monitoring his thoughts becomes a new way to try to prevent the memories from resurfacing, but it only sharpens the focus on the traumatic images. The stronger his threat response, the more he believes he is weak, which in turn fuels the self‑blame that made the crash happen in the first place. The memory that he cannot explain clearly drives his thought‑monitoring because he feels a need to verify that his recollection is accurate, and the memory’s alien quality only deepens his belief that he is not a capable medic. The cycle tightens. His constant threat vigilance makes the world feel hostile; he becomes startled by the hum of a car’s engine on a quiet street, and this startle, in turn, heightens his alertness for triggers such as the scent of alcohol. He avoids driving entirely, preferring buses that, while slower, force him to sit in the back and listen to other passengers’ conversations, many of whom drink and talk about beers, creating new environmental triggers. By shunning the driver’s seat he also removes the comforting routine of a familiar vehicle’s interior, forcing him to seek refuge in settings that reinforce his threat system. Each time he is confronted with a trigger, his body’s physical reactivity spikes, which makes him monitor his thoughts more intensely. The monitoring, in turn, brings back the vivid, alien memory of the crash, strengthening his sense of weakness and self‑blame, which then magnifies the threat he feels to any situation that might remind him of the accident. His avoidance of driving also limits his ability to see that he is safe, making the threat response more entrenched. Now, nearly a decade after the collision, Daniel can barely drive without a surge of panic, and the thought of stepping into a car’s cockpit sends his heart racing and his hands trembling. He has stopped attending his regular volunteer shifts at the veterans’ center, fearing the smell of gas and the echo of metal from a nearby traffic stop. The daily reality of his avoidance has made his social circles smaller, and he feels increasingly isolated, which fuels his negative appraisal that he is weak and incapable of contributing. The memory of the crash, still vivid in his mind and constantly resurfacing through the triggers he encounters in the city, keeps his body in a state of hyperarousal. The thought‑monitoring he has adopted to ward off the terror has only amplified the memory’s alien quality, deepening his self‑blame. He finally seeks help because he can no longer function in the day‑to‑day demands of the world, and his greatest fear is that he will lose his ability to care for others entirely. He hopes to reclaim a sense of control over his thoughts and over the memories that haunt him, believing that if he can break the loop of threat, triggers, and negative appraisal, he might finally feel that he is not weak, but simply human.
